items.title: System One for Tool Approvals
items.summary: Being prompted by an agent before it runs a tool is something many people can relate to nowadays. Common coding agent harnesses ship approval prompts of different granularity and intrusiveness, and adjacent tooling like the Agentic Identity Broker (AIB) that I co-maintain can also hold a tool call until a person approves based on a short description of the tool call. As much as this is a commodity, it is also a controversial feature. Public numbers and my own experience observing myself, friends, family and colleagues suggest that people approve nearly everything they are shown. An approval prompt that is answered by reflex protects little, but still interrupts the agent’s session flow. It seems fair to assume that most approval prompts should never reach a human, and the few that do should be the most critical ones and carry sufficient information to make a truly informed decision. Fewer requests mean less noise, and with that hopefully less approval fatigue. Riding the Jev model wave, I proposed a smarter tool approval approach to AIB: a fast “System One” model could read the actual arguments of a tool call and answer a few narrow questions about them. These answers could then feed into a predefined operator policy that auto-approves harmless calls, and only exceptionally prompts the human user for approval. The idea is similar to the auto mode in Claude Code, where a safety check in the background replaces most permission prompts. None of this is built yet, and before I start I’d like to explore where the design and its UX break. People Approve Nearly Every Tool Call They Are Shown # The best public numbers on reflex approvals I know of come from Anthropic. When they made auto mode the default in Claude Code , they shared that their usage data shows that Claude Code users approve 97% of permission prompts. Anthropic also ran a controlled study with 1,053 paid testers and swapped a single prompt per session for a clearly dangerous command. The testers caught that command in 143 of 1,053 sessions, which is 13.6%. They also got worse over time: early in a session they blocked about 17% of the dangerous commands, and after 50 or more prompts about 5%. Our own AIB gives the approver little to work with today. The Open Policy Agent (OPA) policy that sends a call to approval can attach a description and a risk_level , and that level is currently the only risk signal the approver gets. It is static per tool. A tool like drive.share_file is medium whether the agent shares a file with a colleague or hands editor rights to thirdparty.example.com . A policy author could write rules about single arguments, because OPA receives the arguments of the call. But someone would have to write such a rule for every tool and every argument that matters, and I don’t see that happening when we face an ever-growing number of evolving Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools. The Model Answers Questions and a Policy Auto-Approves # A System One decision model doesn’t generate text. It takes some content and a set of typed questions, and it returns typed answers with probabilities. TypeSafe AI coined the term in September 2026 when it announced Jev. The following is an illustrative example I wrote against a local winnow:e4b , an open-weights System One model that I run with Ollaya : File: Request to a System One model for a tool approval curl http://localhost:11435/v1/systemone -d '{ "model": "winnow:e4b", "state": { "mcp_server": "google-drive-mcp", "tool_name": "drive.share_file", "policy_risk_level": "medium", "arguments": { "role": "editor", "grantee_domain": "thirdparty.example.com", "transfer_ownership": false } }, "questions": { "leaves_organisation": { "type": "noul", "instructions": "Does this call give access or data to a party outside the organisation?" }, "changes_access": { "type": "noul", "instructions": "Does this call change who can access a resource?" }, "reversibility": { "type": "score", "criteria": [ "no persistent effect", "reversible with effort", "irreversible or externally visible" ] } } }' File: Response from the System One model for a tool approval { "model" : "winnow:e4b" , "answers" : { "leaves_organisation" : { "type" : "noul" , "noul" : 0.989 }, "changes_access" : { "type" : "noul" , "noul" : 0.9591 }, "reversibility" : { "type" : "score" , "score" : 1.6509 , "confidence" : 0.5461 , "legend" : { "0" : "no persistent effect" , "1" : "reversible with effort" , "2" : "irreversible or externally visible" }, "probabilities" : { "0" : 0.0465 , "1" : 0.256 , "2" : 0.6974 } } }, "usage" : { "input_tokens" : 462 , "output_tokens" : 0 } } The model gets the tool, the policy’s risk level and the arguments. Running the model locally, close to the broker, keeps these arguments inside the organisation. A noul question is a yes/no question, and the model returns the probability that the answer is yes. A score question places the content on an ordered scale that the caller defines. In this case, we want a good model to return a probability close to 1 for the first two questions and a score in the upper half of the scale, because editor rights for an outside party are externally visible. The answers would be an additional input for the OPA policy and enable a rule that auto-approves any call where both probabilities are close to 0 and the score reads “no persistent effect”. The beauty of this approach is that the model only answers questions while the approval itself is still a deterministic rule in a policy that can be reviewed and reasoned about. “Auto-approve when nothing leaves the organisation and the call has no persistent effect” is a sentence a security team can agree to, test and find again in an audit log next to the answers that triggered it. Limiting what a prompt injection can achieve is another good reason for this approach. The arguments of a tool call are externally controlled content, so the model reading them can be manipulated. A narrow output doesn’t prevent that, but it limits the damage: injected text can skew two numbers and a score, but it can’t smuggle instructions downstream or argue for its own approval, because the policy makes the decision. Fixed answers also help to shape the UX of the approval screen. OWASP’s guidance on Human-Agent Trust Exploitation (ASI09) asks for a “plain-language risk summary (not model-generated rationales)”. “Gives editor access to thirdparty.example.com” is such a summary. A paragraph in which a model explains why the call is probably fine is the persuasive text that the OWASP entry warns about, and a System One model can’t write one. This approach is also not new. Auto modes in modern harnesses commonly have the same goal. Instead of prompting the user, a classifier checks each tool call in the background and blocks the risky ones. Anthropic reports that the classifier blocked 89% of the dangerous commands in the study above, so a model that reads every call clearly beats a fatigued human. The difference is who decides. In auto mode the classifier allows or blocks. The broker sits between many agents and many MCP servers in an organisation, and its operators or auditors have to explain why a call went through without a person. Fixed questions and a verifiable policy give them that explanation. A Failing Model Never Approves Anything # The model will be unreachable at times, it will return answers that don’t parse, and its answers will be uncertain or contradict each other. In all of these cases the request stays what it was before the model existed: a pending approval for the human in the loop. How the broker will detect an uncertain answer isn’t something I have specified yet, but a probability near the middle is one candidate. What is abundantly clear though is that a model’s answers must never turn a policy denial into an approval. The same holds for a permanent denial that a person has set for a tool, which the broker’s approval API already puts above any matching approval. So we want the model to only take approvals off a person for calls that this person would have been allowed to approve anyway. The worst outcome of an outage is today’s approval page and an interrupted agent session. What Is Still Open Before I Build It # Keeping the approval pending covers a model that is down or unsure, but it doesn’t cover a model that is confidently wrong. When that happens, a call goes through that a person might have stopped. So everything depends on the questions you ask, the thresholds in the policy, and a good eval harness that shows how often the model gets recorded tool calls wrong. My three questions are a first guess. Without such evals I can’t tell which questions hold up across actual MCP tools and real tool approval scenarios, or how close to 0 a probability has to be before a rule may skip the person. If you operate tool approvals for agents and know a call that my three questions would let pass although a person should have seen it, please add it to issue #206 . I’d also like to hear which questions you’d want answered before a call may skip you.

 "arguments": {

 "grantee_domain": "thirdparty.example.com",
 "transfer_ownership": false
 }
 },

 "leaves_organisation": {
 "type": "noul",
 "instructions": "Does this call give access or data to a party outside the organisation?"
 },
 "changes_access": {
 "type": "noul",
 "instructions": "Does this call change who can access a resource?"

 "type": "score",
 "criteria": [
 "no persistent effect",
 "reversible with effort",
 "irreversible or externally visible"
 ]

 "type": "noul",

items.title: HU Berlin Talk: AppSec and Agentic Engineering
items.summary: Guest lecture for the Software Engineering course at Humboldt University Berlin (HU) on 16 November 2026. Materials # Slides (PDF) Supporting essay: How Agentic Engineering Puts AppSec Teams Under Pressure Earlier version: HTW Berlin Talk , July 2026 Reading companion # Agentic engineering puts AppSec teams under pressure from two sides. Detection got cheap, so maintainers and AppSec teams get more findings than they can triage and fix, and agents add new attack vectors such as Clinejection, where an issue title led an AI triage agent toward the publish tokens of the coding agent Cline. At the same time, reactive security gates are too slow for agent loops. The lecture looks at the harness first: feedback in the session and security skills might help less than expected when they only cover general security knowledge, and the agent itself needs a sandbox that each developer still configures locally. The platform is likely the better place, as it can take whole decisions away, for example authentication and credentials. For the findings that remain, a risk budget tells people and agents to fix what is reachable first. The lecture closes with three open problems for students and research. This is a short reading companion, not a transcript. The supporting essay follows the storyline of the lecture. Reading list # The sources for the numbers, quotes and examples on the slides, in the order of the talk. Part 1: Clinejection # Adnan Khan, Clinejection: Compromising Cline’s Production Releases just by Prompting an Issue Triager , 9 Feb 2026 (updated 18 Feb 2026). Original research, workflow excerpt and timeline. Snyk, How “Clinejection” Turned an AI Bot into a Supply Chain Attack . Attack chain step by step. Part 2: Detection got cheap # Anthropic, Project Glasswing: An initial update , 22 May 2026. VulnCheck, The Anthropic Glasswing Receipts Are Starting to Trickle In , 8 Sept 2026. Findings, disclosure ledger, fixes and the two severity ratings. Axios, AI bug reports are overwhelming OpenSSL security maintainers , 20 Oct 2026. Cloud Security Alliance, The Disclosure Bottleneck: When AI Discovery Outpaces Patch Consumption , 6 Nov 2026. Part 3: Shift left into the harness # Addy Osmani, Shubham Saboo, Sokratis Kartakis, The New SDLC With Vibe Coding , Google, 2026. Summary by Addy Osmani: The New Software Lifecycle , 16 June 2026. CoSAI, Project CodeGuard : CodeGuard 1.4.0 on SecurityEval , methodology and limits , eval harness . Sandbox documentation: Codex , Cursor run modes , GitHub Copilot local sandbox, generally available , Claude Code sandboxed Bash tool , Claude Code: Choose a sandbox environment . OpenCode has no built-in sandbox: security policy . Add-ons: opencode-sandbox , @hamzaabili/opencode-sandbox , nono profile for OpenCode . pi has no built-in sandbox: Run Pi in an isolated environment . Add-ons: the sandbox example extension , the Gondolin example extension, pi-enclave . Sandboxes to wrap an agent in: nono , Firecracker microVMs . Jazz Security, What is an AI agent sandbox? , 10 Nov 2026. Comparison of the defaults for each agent. Novee, The Sandbox Is a Suggestion: Breaking Claude Code, Gemini CLI, and Codex Sandboxes , 8 Sept 2026. Part 4: Shift down # Kubernetes SIG Security, Shifting Down Security . Endor Labs, Inside the Bitwarden CLI supply chain attack , 23 Apr 2026. Aviatrix, AI Coding Agents Hijacked via AGENTS.md in Downloads Folder , 25 Oct 2026. Vendor report, not the original research. Simon Willison, The lethal trifecta for AI agents , 16 June 2025. Jan Brennenstuhl, Agent Substrate Knows Which Agent Is Calling, but Not for Whom , 9 Nov 2026. Google, Powering open infrastructure for autonomous agents , 5 Nov 2026. Donation of Agent Substrate to the CNCF. Model Context Protocol, The 2026-07-28 Specification , 28 July 2026. Jan Brennenstuhl, Measuring How MCP Servers Authorize Agents , 2 Nov 2026. Jan Brennenstuhl, Shift Down: Why Agentic Engineering Demands Platform-Level Security . Part 5: Measuring risk # Google, Embracing Risk , Site Reliability Engineering book. Error budgets. Regulation (EU) 2024/2847 (Cyber Resilience Act), Article 14. European Commission: CRA reporting . Help Net Security, ENISA launched the CRA Single Reporting Platform , 14 Sept 2026. More # OWASP GenAI Security Project, OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications for 2026 , Dec 2025. Vocabulary for agent risks. Jan Brennenstuhl, AppSec in the Age of Agentic Engineering .

items.title: Memory Palaces, the Major System, and PAO
items.summary: In my review of Moonwalking with Einstein , I promised to follow up on building and maintaining a memory palace, learning the Major System, and building out a full PAO dictionary, along with what stuck after trying each one. All three build on ideas Foer returns to throughout the book. We remember places, faces, and strange images far better than abstract numbers or vocabulary lists, and new information sticks better when attached to structures we already know. Each technique approaches this differently, converting abstract information into something visual, spatial, or familiar that we can use for recall. I built three small tools to practice these ideas and am hosting them for others to try: major.lockboxx.org - Major System and PAO practice palace.lockboxx.org - Designing and walking memory palaces lang.lockboxx.org - Foreign language vocabulary study The Major System converts numbers into words by mapping each digit to a consonant sound: 0 is s/z, 1 is t/d, 2 is n, 3 is m, 4 is r, 5 is l, 6 is j/sh/ch, 7 is k/hard g, 8 is f/v, and 9 is p/b. Vowels and the letters w, h, and y are ignored, allowing you to fill in the sounds to make words. Small hooks make the mappings easier to learn (n has two downstrokes for 2, m has three for 3), and learning them in pairs helped me remember all ten. The app at major.lockboxx.org drills these mappings by having you decode words back into digits, starting with a simplified first-letter system before moving into traditional two-digit pegs like sauce for 00 and tuna for 12. Puzzles are seeded so you can replay or share them, with the answer key always available. PAO (Person-Action-Object) extends the idea by assigning a person, action, and object to every number from 00 through 99, creating roughly 300 dictionary entries. Six digits then become a single scene, combining the person from the first pair, action from the second, and object from the third. In the app's Medium PAO mode, 147049 becomes the bizarre image "Thor kiss rope". Any phone number then becomes 5 short words in one memorable phrase. The memory palace, or method of loci , uses a familiar place and a fixed route through distinct anchor points to store information. You associate each item with an exaggerated image at an anchor, then mentally walk the route to recall them in order. Keeping the route one-directional, spacing anchors apart, and making the images absurd helps prevent them from blurring together. Palaces also need maintenance, including retiring heavily used ones temporarily and reviewing others on a schedule (a day later, three days, a week, two weeks). I built palace.lockboxx.org to design and visualize these structures, and it grew into something close to build mode from the old Sims games. You generate a house from a seed in several styles (condos, family homes, mansions, and Frank Lloyd Wright-style Prairie houses), then edit rooms, walls, doors, and furniture. Anchors are placed on furniture, and the app suggests a route that enters through the front door and keeps turning right, room by room and floor by floor. You can walk through in first person, tour between anchors, or use recall mode to hide notes until you reveal them. The entire palace is stored in its URL, making structures easy to share. The last idea I applied was chunking, the idea that expertise is built from existing groups of knowledge and that new information is easier to remember when attached to those groups. I applied this to language learning with lang.lockboxx.org , a vocabulary game where you choose word pools, difficulty, and a seed before working through three stages: learning the words, drilling them through different exercises (meaning, reverse, listening, fill-in-the-blank, typing), and writing your own sentences. Rather than generic textbook lists, I built vocabulary pools around things I already know well. The Japanese and French pools include Magic: The Gathering keywords, card zones, rules text, and anime battle and fantasy vocabulary. I play with a lot of Japanese cards, so I also loaded vocabulary from specific anime subtitles I've been watching. After reading a card a thousand times in English, I have an existing structure to attach the Japanese or French version to. The biggest takeaway for me was how differently these approaches worked in practice. The Major System was much easier to learn than I expected, becoming almost automatic within a few days of practice. Within weeks, door codes, phone numbers, and dates became easier to remember, and having a phonetic handle for numbers helped with everyday recall. I even found myself quantizing more things around the house and committing them to memory, although I'm not sure that was directly related. PAO also worked well when applied to systems I already knew. The memory palace was the most fun to build but the one I've practiced the least. I'm into houses and remodeling, so I've admittedly spent more time designing floor plans than memorizing with them. I also really enjoyed making the language app practical, and I'm hoping the vocabulary sticks better because I regularly encounter it in material I already know. I like Duolingo's gamified approach to language learning, and tying that kind of practice to hobbies I already care about seems like the most practical application of the book's ideas for my own life.

In my review of Moonwalking with Einstein, I promised to follow up on building and maintaining a memory palace, learning the Major System, and building out a full PAO dictionary, along with what stuck after trying each one. All three build on ideas Foer returns to throughout the book. We remember places, faces, and strange images far better than abstract numbers or vocabulary lists, and new information sticks better when attached to structures we already know. Each technique approaches this differently, converting abstract information into something visual, spatial, or familiar that we can use for recall. I built three small tools to practice these ideas and am hosting them for others to try:

  • major.lockboxx.org - Major System and PAO practice
  • palace.lockboxx.org - Designing and walking memory palaces
  • lang.lockboxx.org - Foreign language vocabulary study

The Major System converts numbers into words by mapping each digit to a consonant sound: 0 is s/z, 1 is t/d, 2 is n, 3 is m, 4 is r, 5 is l, 6 is j/sh/ch, 7 is k/hard g, 8 is f/v, and 9 is p/b. Vowels and the letters w, h, and y are ignored, allowing you to fill in the sounds to make words. Small hooks make the mappings easier to learn (n has two downstrokes for 2, m has three for 3), and learning them in pairs helped me remember all ten. The app at major.lockboxx.org drills these mappings by having you decode words back into digits, starting with a simplified first-letter system before moving into traditional two-digit pegs like sauce for 00 and tuna for 12. Puzzles are seeded so you can replay or share them, with the answer key always available. PAO (Person-Action-Object) extends the idea by assigning a person, action, and object to every number from 00 through 99, creating roughly 300 dictionary entries. Six digits then become a single scene, combining the person from the first pair, action from the second, and object from the third. In the app's Medium PAO mode, 147049 becomes the bizarre image "Thor kiss rope". Any phone number then becomes 5 short words in one memorable phrase. 

The memory palace, or method of loci, uses a familiar place and a fixed route through distinct anchor points to store information. You associate each item with an exaggerated image at an anchor, then mentally walk the route to recall them in order. Keeping the route one-directional, spacing anchors apart, and making the images absurd helps prevent them from blurring together. Palaces also need maintenance, including retiring heavily used ones temporarily and reviewing others on a schedule (a day later, three days, a week, two weeks). I built palace.lockboxx.org to design and visualize these structures, and it grew into something close to build mode from the old Sims games. You generate a house from a seed in several styles (condos, family homes, mansions, and Frank Lloyd Wright-style Prairie houses), then edit rooms, walls, doors, and furniture. Anchors are placed on furniture, and the app suggests a route that enters through the front door and keeps turning right, room by room and floor by floor. You can walk through in first person, tour between anchors, or use recall mode to hide notes until you reveal them. The entire palace is stored in its URL, making structures easy to share.

The last idea I applied was chunking, the idea that expertise is built from existing groups of knowledge and that new information is easier to remember when attached to those groups. I applied this to language learning with lang.lockboxx.org, a vocabulary game where you choose word pools, difficulty, and a seed before working through three stages: learning the words, drilling them through different exercises (meaning, reverse, listening, fill-in-the-blank, typing), and writing your own sentences. Rather than generic textbook lists, I built vocabulary pools around things I already know well. The Japanese and French pools include Magic: The Gathering keywords, card zones, rules text, and anime battle and fantasy vocabulary. I play with a lot of Japanese cards, so I also loaded vocabulary from specific anime subtitles I've been watching. After reading a card a thousand times in English, I have an existing structure to attach the Japanese or French version to.

The biggest takeaway for me was how differently these approaches worked in practice. The Major System was much easier to learn than I expected, becoming almost automatic within a few days of practice. Within weeks, door codes, phone numbers, and dates became easier to remember, and having a phonetic handle for numbers helped with everyday recall. I even found myself quantizing more things around the house and committing them to memory, although I'm not sure that was directly related. PAO also worked well when applied to systems I already knew. The memory palace was the most fun to build but the one I've practiced the least. I'm into houses and remodeling, so I've admittedly spent more time designing floor plans than memorizing with them. I also really enjoyed making the language app practical, and I'm hoping the vocabulary sticks better because I regularly encounter it in material I already know. I like Duolingo's gamified approach to language learning, and tying that kind of practice to hobbies I already care about seems like the most practical application of the book's ideas for my own life.

items.title: Researchers Find Six 0-Days Allowing Unauthorized Takeover of Supermarket Refrigeration Systems
items.summary: Six pre-authentication remote code execution flaws were found in the Danfoss AK-SM800A supermarket fridge controller, allowing remote takeover in about an hour, according to Midnight Blue researcher Carlo Meijer. The flaws are stack-based buffer overflows. They affect every firmware version up to and including 5.3.2, and no CVE numbers have been assigned yet. Since October 11, waves of cyber attacks have hit internet-exposed Danfoss and Copeland fridge controllers across Europe. Attackers started defrost cycles, and the losses reached tens of millions of euros. Some stores even had fires, according to Wikipedia’s incident summary. Cyber Security News has followed the story from the start, including its report on the 4,980 exposed Danfoss hosts . Who is behind the incidents is still debated. France has blamed Iran’s Shahid Kaveh unit, but SentinelOne says attribution remains open and the incidents may not share one operator. The French agency ANSSI also said its early findings pointed to exposed admin pages and weak passwords, not the older published bugs. Meijer did not use fuzzing or AI. He downloaded the public firmware, ran the main program in an emulator, and looked for places where the code calls strcpy. This old C function copies data without checking its size, so a long input can overflow memory. One unauthenticated web handler crashed after he sent a long string of “A” characters. He found at least five bugs of this kind in a small part of the code. The binary also lacked stack canaries and PIE, two basic protections that make such bugs harder to use. The program runs as root, so a successful exploit gives full control. Supermarket Fridge Controller Takeover Midnight Blue showed a working root exploit on an older firmware version. The team is withholding technical details while it works with Danfoss on coordinated disclosure. Danfoss added session control in later firmware, and “strict” became the default from version 4.0. This setting blocks most of the web attack surface for unauthenticated users, and CERT-FR lists it among its official mitigations. Even so, the researchers found another overflow in sm_fcgi_app, the component that checks logins, and it still works on the latest firmware with strict mode on. The team also warns about what comes after a break-in. The controller does not use the i.MX6 chip’s secure boot features. An attacker with root access could therefore plant an implant that survives a factory reset. They could also wipe the flash memory or push bad firmware to brick the device. That would force stores to replace hardware, and freezers could sit idle for days. Midnight Blue compares this to the wiper-style tactics seen in the December 2025 attack on the Polish electric grid . The researchers say patching one bug at a time is a poor use of limited staff time. Owners should find every exposed controller, including those behind integrators’ 4G modems. They should then move remote access behind a VPN, a private APN, or a strict IP allow list. CERT-FR warns that allow lists are only a short-term fix. Exposure is still high. Censys sees hundreds of Danfoss devices online, plus over 1,000 Copeland and Dixell units. Earlier Cyber Security News coverage of Copeland XWEB Pro flaws showed the same pattern. Until these controllers leave the open internet, new bugs will keep putting food and medicine at risk. items.title: Race Against the (Mac)hine: Local Privilege Escalation in Microsoft Defender for macOS
items.summary: Patching a vulnerability in cross-platform software can be tricky. At BlueHat Asia in September, I presented on two LPEs I found in Microsoft Defender that arose from differences in operating system-level security and filesystem APIs that broke critical security assumptions (CVE-2026-50657, CVE-2026-50658).
